title: Phase distinction of Gibbs states without symmetry breaking: topological invariants of the 3D toric code
abstract: We study the finite-temperature topological order of the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code in a generic magnetic field, where every higher-form symmetry is explicitly broken and can at most be emergent. We show perturbatively, and confirm by large-scale quantum Monte Carlo, that the topological entanglement entropy stays quantized at $γ= \ln 2$ throughout the topological phase -- at finite temperature and under the symmetry-breaking field alike -- and collapses to $0$ across the thermal transition, a quantization protected geometrically by the Bianchi identity rather than by any exact symmetry of the system. The plateau $γ= \ln 2$ is, however, not invariant under quasi-local channels: a constant-depth channel can generate this identical quantized value from a trivial product state. We therefore introduce the decoded Wilson-loop correlation $f_W$, which quantizes to $1$ in the topological phase and $0$ in the trivial phase as $L\to\infty$ and, unlike $γ$, is a quasi-local-channel invariant -- a robust topological invariant of the mixed state.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of identifying topological phases at finite temperature without relying on symmetry breaking. By analyzing the 3D $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code, the authors introduce a novel, robust order parameter called $f_W$. This invariant successfully distinguishes between topologically ordered and trivial phases across complex field-temperature regimes where traditional measures fail.
main_problem: The central problem is determining if sharp phase distinctions can be identified for topological order at non-zero temperature ($T>0$) without relying on spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB). The authors seek robust, quasi-local-channel invariants to classify these mixed states.
main_result: A new diagnostic, the decoded Wilson-loop correlation $f_W$, is introduced and shown to be a robust invariant that quantizes to 1 in the topological phase and 0 in the trivial phase at finite temperature. This distinguishes phases where traditional measures like entanglement entropy ($\gamma$) fail.
method: The study combines perturbative calculations, large-scale Quantum Monte Carlo simulations on the thermal Gibbs state, and theoretical analysis of various correlation functions (Wilson loops, string order parameters).
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the three-dimensional ($	ext{3D}$) $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code subjected to generic magnetic fields and finite temperature. The Hamiltonian/Gibbs measure describes the thermal state $ho_ eta = e^{- eta \hat{H}/Z}$.
key_observables: Topological Entanglement Entropy ($\gamma$), Decoded Wilson-loop correlation ($f_W$), Fredenhagen–Marcu string order parameter ($ho_{	ext{FM}}$), and various thermodynamic responses like specific heat ($C_v$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), external magnetic fields $(h_x, h_z)$, and the lattice size $L$. The critical point is often compared to the 3D Ising universality class.
main_assumptions: The authors must contend with the ambiguity of phase equivalence relations for Gibbs states at $T>0$, sometimes assuming quasi-static traversal through Lindbladian channels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how different observables (Wilson loops, $ho_{	ext{FM}}$) show differential sensitivity to magnetic, electric, and thermal fields across the $(h_x, h_z, T)$ phase diagram. Table I summarizes diagnostic values for various models.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares multiple diagnostics ($\gamma$, Wilson loops, etc.) against known transitions (thermal $T_c$, magnetic $h_x^c$, electric $h_z^c$). It culminates in the proposal and rigorous demonstration of $f_W$ as the universal invariant resolving all three boundaries.
why_interesting: The work provides a powerful, non-symmetry-breaking diagnostic tool ($f_W$) for characterizing topological order in realistic thermal settings, which is crucial for understanding quantum phase transitions in condensed matter systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The three tiers of states and their phase-equivalence relations. Pure gapped ground states (bottom) are classified by finite-depth local unitaries—equivalently, quasi-adiabatic continuation along a path of local Hamiltonians with no gap closing [15, 16]. General mixed states (top) are classified by two-way quasi-local channels [17–19]. The intermediate Gibbs tier is classified by a path of local Hamiltonians with no ther- modynamic singularity.
